clinician.trajectory_summary: A 31-year-old woman with known Child's B liver cirrhosis and portal hypertension presented with a one-month history of dull left hypochondriac abdominal pain. On admission, she had documented cytopenias (WBC 1.9 x 10^9/L, platelets 54 x 10^9/L) and Hackett's Grade 2 splenomegaly. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a saccular splenic artery aneurysm (SAA) measuring 3.4 x 3.4 x 4.3 cm with thrombus and splenic infarction, which explained the localized left hypochondriac pain. The patient underwent successful angiographic coiling of the SAA using fibered angiocoils and lipiodol embolization material. Follow-up laboratory studies demonstrated dramatic improvement in blood counts: WBC increased from 1.9 to 5.0 x 10^9/L and platelets increased from 54 to 209 x 10^9/L. Follow-up CT imaging showed splenic size reduction from 10.8 x 7.4 x 18.6 cm to 9.3 x 5.4 x 16.1 cm. The cytopenias were secondary to hypersplenism caused by the combination of cirrhosis-related portal hypertension and the splenic pathology (aneurysm with infarction). The rapid resolution of cytopenias and splenic size reduction after embolization confirmed the hypersplenism diagnosis.

Successful angiographic coiling of the SAA performed using fibered angiocoils and lipiodol embolization
Follow-up laboratory studies showed improvement: WBC increased from 1.9 to 5.0 x 10^9/L and platelets increased from 54 to 209 x 10^9/L
Follow-up CT imaging demonstrated splenic size reduction from 10.8 x 7.4 x 18.6 cm to 9.3 x 5.4 x 16.1 cm

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.alternative: Primary aplastic anemia (severe aplastic anemia as primary bone marrow failure)
ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: The dramatic improvement in blood counts (WBC from 1.9 to 5.0, platelets from 54 to 209) following SAA embolization and the concurrent reduction in splenic size strongly indicate that cytopenias were secondary to hypersplenism rather than primary bone marrow failure. Primary aplastic anemia would not show such rapid hematologic recovery with splenic intervention alone.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.alternative: Isolated hypersplenism from cirrhosis without structural splenic pathology
ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: The imaging findings of a saccular splenic artery aneurysm with thrombus and splenic infarction demonstrate structural splenic pathology beyond simple portal hypertension-related hypersplenism. The aneurysm and infarction are the anatomic basis for the exaggerated hypersplenism in this patient.

remaining_uncertainties: Hemoglobin and hematocrit values from admission CBC and follow-up studies were not documented in available source records, so the complete pancytopenia picture (including anemia component) could not be verified
Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy results were not documented, so direct confirmation of normocellular/hypercellular marrow (ruling out primary aplastic anemia) could not be obtained
Peripheral blood smear findings and reticulocyte count were not documented
WBC differential assessment was not documented
Specific temporal details of abdominal pain resolution after embolization were not documented
The etiology of the splenic artery aneurysm development in the setting of cirrhosis was not explicitly discussed in available records
